title: A Mysterious Object in Our Galaxy Has Been Emitting a Radio Signal for Two Decades — and Nobody Can Explain Why
excerpt: An international team of astronomers has published a detailed study of VT J1906+0849, a radio source discovered in the VLASS survey (Very Large Array Sky Survey) that doesn't resemble anything else previously catalogued in the Milky Way. content:
For more than twenty years, something in the Milky Way has been broadcasting radio waves without fading, without expanding, and without matching any known type of object in our galaxy.

An international team of astronomers has published a detailed study of VT J1906+0849, a radio source discovered in the VLASS survey (Very Large Array Sky Survey) that doesn’t resemble anything else previously catalogued in the Milky Way. The paper, led by Jessie M. Miller of the California Institute of Technology, combines radio, infrared, optical, and X-ray observations in an attempt to pin down what the object actually is.

VT J1906+0849 first stood out as a radio transient: something that switched on where nothing had been seen before. It showed up in the first epoch of the VLASS survey, on October 27, 2017, glowing at about 70 millijanskys (mJy) at 3 GHz — a standard unit astronomers use to measure how bright a radio source is. The striking part is what came before that: 21 years earlier, in 1996, an earlier survey called NVSS had scanned the exact same patch of sky and found nothing there.

That non-detection sets a hard floor: whatever this object is, it brightened by a factor of at least six over two decades. That alone made it the brightest transient ever found in VLASS.

When the team went back through older radio archives, the picture got stranger. They turned up more than 30 separate detections going back to 2005. The source, it turned out, had been quietly active since 2005, climbed to a peak above 200 mJy in 2014, faded for several years, and then brightened again in late 2025 — twenty years of on-again, off-again glowing that shows no sign of stopping. The object sits at a galactic latitude of roughly 0.74 degrees, almost exactly on the plane of the Milky Way’s disk.

How far away is it?

Pinning down the distance was the first order of business, because it determines whether VT J1906+0849 belongs to our galaxy at all. The team used a classic technique: measuring how cold hydrogen gas along the line of sight absorbs part of the object’s radio signal at the 21-centimeter wavelength.

The pattern of absorption showed that the source sits behind gas located beyond the Norma-Cygnus spiral arm — one of the Milky Way’s major structural arms, roughly on the opposite side of the galaxy from Earth.

That places VT J1906+0849 at a minimum of 15,000 parsecs away (about 49,000 light-years), and possibly as far as 32,000 parsecs (roughly 104,000 light-years) — for comparison, that’s farther than the distance from Earth to the galactic center, about 26,000 light-years. At that range, the object sits in the Milky Way’s warped, thickened outer disk.

Breaking every rule in the book

What makes VT J1906+0849 genuinely strange is not any single measurement, but the combination. In radio, it has been emitting continuously for two decades — not the signature of a one-off explosion, which would flare and fade. Its radio spectrum peaks at a frequency that shifts back and forth unpredictably: 1.9 GHz in 2019, down to 0.8 GHz in 2024, then back up to 2.2 GHz in 2026. That kind of back-and-forth doesn’t fit a simple picture of an expanding cloud of particles cooling down.

The real anomaly, though, comes from the VLBA, a continent-spanning network of radio dishes capable of resolving extremely fine detail. Those observations show the emitting region is remarkably compact — just a few astronomical units across (one astronomical unit, or AU, is the distance from Earth to the Sun, about 150 million kilometers or 93 million miles).

Between 2010 and 2025, that region barely grew at all. The inferred expansion speed is under 10 kilometers per second, and possibly closer to just 1 kilometer per second — extraordinarily slow for something powered by particles accelerated to relativistic speeds. For context, a typical young supernova remnant expands at several thousand kilometers per second; this object is moving hundreds of times slower than that.

The brightness temperature — a measure of how energetic the emission mechanism must be — tops 100 million kelvin (about six times hotter than the core of the Sun, which sits around 15 million kelvin), ruling out ordinary thermal glow. Instead, the signal is synchrotron radiation: light produced by electrons spiraling at close to the speed of light around magnetic field lines.

Near-infrared observations from the Keck Observatory in Hawaii turned up a single broad emission line near 2.14 micrometers, present in every observation between 2021 and 2026. Its position on the spectrum never moves, but its width and brightness do.

Astronomers interpret it as a hydrogen emission line (known as Brackett-gamma, or Brγ) that has been shifted toward the blue end of the spectrum — a telltale sign that gas is racing toward us, in this case at roughly 2,600 kilometers per second, or close to 1 percent of the speed of light. The width of the line implies velocities ranging from 1,400 to 2,220 kilometers per second.

What the object looks like in optical and infrared light

The optical and infrared counterpart is just as puzzling. It shows up faintly in archival images from Pan-STARRS, UKIDSS, Spitzer, and WISE. Its brightness hasn’t changed meaningfully in more than a decade, which rules out a supernova or any other one-time explosion.

Modeling its light output suggests a hot star, with a surface temperature above 10,000 kelvin, wrapped in a disk or envelope of dust. That dust radiates at most 15 percent of the star’s total light output in the infrared.

Interstellar dust in that direction of the sky is unusually thick, dimming the object by 11 to 14 magnitudes in visible light — equivalent to blocking tens of thousands of times more light than would otherwise reach us. Without correcting for that extinction, the object would be invisible from Earth.

Ruling out the usual suspects

The team systematically eliminated the more familiar explanations. It isn’t a nova: those brighten in radio for weeks or months, not decades, and nowhere near this luminously. It isn’t a classic pulsar wind nebula either — those evolve over centuries or millennia, while VT J1906+0849 changes noticeably from one year to the next.

A flare star and a typical X-ray binary were both ruled out too, because the Swift X-ray telescope found nothing. The upper limit on its X-ray output, 9×10³³ erg/s, is far below what an X-ray binary with this much radio power would be expected to produce.

An extragalactic origin — a quasar or blazar sitting billions of light-years away rather than inside our own galaxy — looks unlikely as well. Once corrected for dust extinction, the object’s optical spectrum is much bluer than typical quasars, and no other emission lines show up that would let astronomers measure a redshift and confirm a cosmological distance.

As the authors put it, none of these individual clues rules out an extragalactic origin on its own — not the steep optical spectrum, the wavelength and width of that one emission line, nor the radio spectrum’s unpredictable swings on timescales of less than a year. But taken together, they write, the radio behavior restricts a viable extragalactic interpretation primarily to a compact, rapidly evolving, jet-dominated source.

The leading hypothesis: a young SS 433

The explanation that fits the data best, according to the paper, is that VT J1906+0849 is a young cousin of SS 433, a genuinely bizarre binary system in the Milky Way in which a normal star feeds material onto a compact companion — most likely a black hole — producing jets of particles moving at a sizable fraction of the speed of light. In SS 433, a thick accretion disk drives a powerful wind that boxes in those jets, forcing them into a narrow, funnel-shaped outflow rather than letting them spread freely.

One possible interpretation is that VT J1906+0849 is a young analog of the microquasar SS 433, with a dense disk wind confining a continuously powered synchrotron outflow. This jet-wind interaction explains the compact, slowly expanding radio source and may contribute to the absence of bright X-ray emission, the authors conclude.

Under this scenario, a compact object is pulling in material at a high rate, launching a particle jet that produces the synchrotron radio glow. That jet never gets to expand freely because it’s slamming into a dense, lopsided wind blowing off the accretion disk. The wind squeezes the jet into a tiny region, which is why the source hasn’t visibly grown over fifteen years of monitoring.

The part of that wind moving toward Earth produces the blueshifted infrared line; the part moving away is hidden from view. And if the wind is dense enough close to the compact object, it could be absorbing any X-rays before they escape — explaining why Swift saw nothing.

What’s still unknown

The authors are upfront about the open questions. The identification of the infrared line as blueshifted Brγ isn’t certain. It’s also odd that no other hydrogen or helium lines show up, especially compared to the rich, complex spectrum SS 433 itself displays.

Resolving that will take high-resolution, multi-epoch near-infrared spectroscopy, to determine whether the line traces a steady wind, an orbital motion, or something more complicated. Deep observations in hard X-rays would also help settle whether there’s an absorbed central engine hiding just out of reach of Swift’s more limited sensitivity.

VT J1906+0849 highlights the potential of wide-field radio surveys to uncover a population of obscured Galactic accretors that are difficult to identify at other wavelengths, the paper concludes (Miller et al. 2026). Notably, the object was also identified independently by a separate search effort — a coincidence the authors say strengthens confidence that the detection itself is solid, even if its nature remains an open question.
